title: Observation of strong electric dipole-dipole interactions between two atoms
authors: Yu-Kun Lu; Jiahao Lyu; Wolfgang Ketterle
problem: Two atoms closer than the reduced optical wavelength \(\bar\lambda=\lambda/2\pi\) should interact through light much more strongly than they decay: the near-field dipole-dipole coupling grows as \(\hbar\Gamma/(r/\bar\lambda)^{3}\). Seeing this needs densities above \(10^{15}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), where inelastic collisions usually destroy the gas, so light-induced dipolar effects in cold atoms had been seen only in the weak far-field regime, summed over many atoms.
result: With exactly two dysprosium atoms per site of a deep optical lattice, squeezed to an rms size of about 20 nm (peak density \(2\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(n\bar\lambda^{3}>10\)), the authors observe: single-photon emission giving median momentum transfers near \(8\hbar k\), with about 30% of atoms above \(10\hbar k\); a coherent force between laser-dressed dipoles of about 1 debye; and a "two-body Lamb shift" of the resonance, \(8.6\pm2.5\) MHz or \(0.27(8)\Gamma\), when the pair wavefunction is flattened. Simulations without free parameters reproduce the momentum data.
significance: The authors report the first observation of strong light-induced dipolar interaction between two atoms in well-defined states, the minimal system for near-field optical dipole physics, which earlier experiments saw only as a collective, essentially classical effect of thousands of atoms. It opens driven two-body systems with coherent dipolar coupling to study, and sheds light on photoassociation.
limitations: The shift was observed only for one aspect ratio: lattice power did not allow the opposite shape, which should give a blue shift. The measured shift agrees with the model semi-quantitatively (prediction \(0.38\Gamma\) for the doublon-singlon mixture). Some observations, such as the absent extra incoherent scattering and asymmetric losses, are explained by motional dynamics or left as possibilities. Doublon signals are obtained by subtracting a singlon-only measurement. No AI-use statement was found.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-11: the main text through the two-body Lamb shift section and the acknowledgements; the Methods were not read in detail. The densities, the size of the near-field shift, the ratio of shift to linewidth and the angular average of the dipolar interaction were recomputed.
methods_source_section: Main text: atom pairs at high density; large momentum transfer; two-body Lamb shift
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: A single atom coupled to the vacuum gets a Lamb shift and a decay rate \(\Gamma\). Two atoms sharing the vacuum exchange virtual photons, giving a dipole-dipole interaction with a coherent part and a dissipative part. Far apart (\(kr\gg1\)) the interaction is weak and has been seen only as a sum over many atoms, in shifts of dense clouds and in the lensing of a condensate. Close together (\(kr\ll1\)) the coherent part dominates and scales as \(1/(kr)^{3}\).
The question is what two atoms do in that strong near-field regime, where a single excitation shared between them feels a force much larger than a photon recoil.

The authors load a dysprosium condensate into a deep 3D lattice, forming a core of doubly occupied sites in the lowest spin state, where two-body and three-body losses are absent. Exciting both atoms with a fast pulse on the narrow 626 nm line and letting one photon escape leaves the pair in a symmetric single-excitation state, which pushes the atoms apart before the second decay: momenta reach several photon recoils, shrinking as the wavepackets are expanded. Driving off resonance on the 421 nm line dresses each atom with an oscillating dipole of about 1 debye; the pair then exerts a coherent force with little photon scattering. In the fluorescence spectrum, the dipolar shift averages almost to zero for a spherical pair, but flattening the pair so the atoms sit side by side gives a measurable red shift.

Open points are the blue shift for the opposite aspect ratio, the low and asymmetric photoassociation losses, and driven many-body systems with strong coherent dipolar coupling, now accessible at these densities.

methods.technique: Densities in units of the optical wavelength
methods.explanation: Whether the near field dominates is set by the dimensionless density \(n\bar\lambda^{3}\), not by the density alone. Converting the paper's numbers checks that two atoms in a 20 nm wavepacket are deep in the regime where coherent coupling beats spontaneous emission.
math: For two atoms with Gaussian wavepackets of rms size \(\sigma\), the peak density seen by one atom is about \(2/((2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma^{3})\). At \(\sigma=20\) nm this is \(1.6\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), the stated \(2\times10^{16}\). With \(\bar\lambda=\lambda/2\pi\), \[n\bar\lambda^{3}\approx6\ (421\ \mathrm{nm}),\qquad n\bar\lambda^{3}\approx20\ (626\ \mathrm{nm}),\] so the paper's \(n\bar\lambda^{3}>10\) refers to the 626 nm line (editorial check).

The coherent coupling exceeds \(\Gamma\) when \(r<\bar\lambda\approx100\) nm, a density of \(1/(100\ \mathrm{nm})^{3}=10^{15}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), the threshold quoted. The near-field shift scale \(\Gamma/(k\sqrt2\sigma)^{3}\) at \(\sigma=22\) nm and 421 nm is \(10\Gamma\), as stated, so the much smaller measured shift reflects angular cancellation, not weak coupling.
methods.transfer: For any light-matter platform, express separations in units of \(\bar\lambda\) and couplings in units of \(\Gamma\) before comparing regimes; the same atoms can be in the weak collective regime on one transition and the strong pairwise regime on another.

methods.technique: Shaping the pair to reveal an averaged-out shift
methods.explanation: The dipolar interaction is anisotropic, so in a spherical pair it averages to almost nothing even though it is ten linewidths strong locally. Changing the aspect ratio of the pair wavefunction, without changing the cloud as a whole, exposes the shift and separates it from collective effects of the dense cloud.
math: The near-field interaction is \(V_{\mathrm{dd}}\propto(3\cos^{2}\theta-1)/r^{3}\), with \(\theta\) the angle between the quantisation axis and the interatomic axis. Over a sphere \[\tfrac12\int_0^{\pi}(3\cos^{2}\theta-1)\sin\theta\,d\theta=0,\] so only the convolution with the Lorentzian line leaves a small shift. Squeezing the pair vertically makes side-by-side configurations (\(\theta\approx\pi/2\), attractive) more likely and shifts the line to the red.

Measured: no shift for \((\sigma_h,\sigma_z)=(22,26)\) nm and \(8.6\pm2.5\) MHz for \((22,16)\) nm; with \(\Gamma_{421}=2\pi\times32\) MHz this is \(0.27\Gamma\) (editorial ratio). Lattice light shifts, optical-density effects and detuning-dependent losses were each ruled out by separate tests, since the cloud's overall shape was unchanged.
methods.transfer: When an interaction cancels under isotropic averaging, measure a differential signal while deforming only the relative wavefunction; this isolates pairwise physics from bulk effects of the same sample.
